(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

***

**Review: *Monsters vs. Aliens***

**(CNN)** — Prepare yourselves: another extravagantly bloated, hyper-produced, high-concept spectacle has breached the confines of DreamWorks Animation, intent on captivating young audiences. In *Monsters vs. Aliens*, Susan—aka "Ginormica"—is tasked with saving the planet. Yet, there is little cause for true alarm. The film is ultimately a harmless endeavor: a benign satire featuring a reflexive feminist narrative anchored by a painfully tenuous plot. 

Such a critique may sound severe. Admittedly, the prospect of a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on improvised roller skates made of automobiles offers the ultimate demolition derby thrill. Consider that premise for a moment, however: traditional skates function due to fixed wheels, whereas substituting motorized vehicles yields a far less effective result. Is this overly pedantic? Perhaps. Yet one would rarely find Pixar acting so indifferent toward the laws of physics. This oversight reflects a broader, lackadaisical approach to storytelling endemic to DreamWorks’ animated catalog—a feature crafted, incidentally, by a creative talent pool boasting the directors of *Shrek 2* and *Shark Tale*, alongside the writers of *Kung Fu Panda* and *The Rocker*. High-concept premises, star-studded voice casts, and a barrage of pop-culture references cannot compensate for the absence of a coherent script.

The oversized heroine in question—dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military captors—begins as the unassuming, petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon). Her life changes irrevocably when a meteorite strikes her moments before she is to marry Derek (Paul Rudd), an unctuous chauvinist. Her sudden, dramatic growth spurt mercifully spares her from a union worse than death, even if her new companions initially seem little better. These include Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist partially mutated into an insect; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), a mindless, gelatinous blue mass who manages quite well without a brain; the Missing Link (Will Arnett), a bravado-filled, loudmouthed amphibian; and Insectosaurus, a colossal dust mite who remains mute simply because he has nothing to say.

Science-fiction aficionados will take pleasure in identifying homage after homage to cinema classics—ranging from *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*, *Invaders from Mars*, and *The Fly*, to *The Creature from the Black Lagoon*, *The Blob*, *Mothra*, and *Attack of the 50-Foot Woman*. There are also several clever nuances; notably, Kiefer Sutherland’s portrayal of General W.R. Monger offers a sharp riff on George C. Scott’s iconic performance in *Dr. Strangelove*.

Regrettably, once the character introductions conclude, the filmmakers are left to maneuver a desperately lackluster plot. The White House calls upon this monstrous squad to defend Earth from Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a four-eyed, eight-legged, squid-like alien, and his giant, one-eyed metallic minion. Ginormica is granted an empowering climax, emerging as a vastly superior character—in every sense—to the nation's commander-in-chief, who is delightfully voiced by Stephen Colbert in a touch of genuine casting wit. While this choice represents savvy studio marketing and sound politics—given the rarity of truly empowered female leads in mainstream family animation (excluding *Coraline*, which proved far too frightening for my household)—Susan’s burgeoning self-worth takes an inordinately long time to materialize.

*(iReport.com: What is your take on 'Monsters vs. Aliens'?)*

Oddly enough—and perhaps it is merely a trick of the imagination—Gallaxhar bears a curious physical resemblance to President Obama, prompting one to wonder if Susan/Ginormica is meant to serve as an allegorical proxy for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton.

Visually, the film is similarly uninspired, though its artistic deficiencies may be somewhat obscured if viewed in 3-D. It is ironic how three-dimensional cinema so frequently produces two-dimensional characters—with *Coraline* again standing as the notable exception.

Lighthearted and unabashedly pulp, *Monsters vs. Aliens* ought to offer immense entertainment—and, in isolated moments, it delivers. Truthfully, however, the film is as self-absorbed as Susan’s vanity-stricken fiancé. Quite frankly, I found *Space Chimps* to be a more enjoyable experience.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* has a running time of 94 minutes and is rated PG. For *Entertainment Weekly’s* perspective, click here.

**Title:** Size Matters, Script Doesn’t: The Empty Spectacle of DreamWorks’ *Monsters vs. Aliens*

In the late 2000s, animated cinema found itself at a crucial crossroads. On one side stood studios dedicated to rich, emotionally resonant storytelling; on the other stood DreamWorks Animation, a studio often content to trade structural integrity for pop-culture references, celebrity voice casts, and cutting-edge visual gimmicks. Entering the fray with maximum hype and marketed as a groundbreaking 3D event, *Monsters vs. Aliens* (2009) perfectly encapsulates this ideological divide. While it boasts an intriguing high-concept premise and occasional flashes of visual flair, the film ultimately collapses under the weight of an incoherent script and a frustratingly superficial approach to its own themes.

The film’s setup is classic mid-century B-movie fare reimagined through a modern lens. On her wedding day, modest California woman Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon) is struck by a meteor glowing with "Quantonium." The alien element causes her to grow to a staggering fifty feet tall, instantly upending her life and her dreams of marrying a self-absorbed local TV weatherman. Whisked away by the military to a top-secret containment facility, Susan is renamed "Ginormica" and introduced to a ragtag group of government-sequestered misfits: the gelatinous, brainless B.O.B. (Seth Rogen); the mad-scientist hybrid Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D. (Hugh Laurie); the prehistoric fish-man The Missing Link (Will Arnett); and the massive, unintelligible Insectosaurus. When an alien megalomaniac named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) invades Earth to reclaim the Quantonium, the U.S. government deploys this monster squad as humanity’s unlikely last line of defense.

On paper, this pitch promises a delightfully chaotic blend of 1950s sci-fi nostalgia and modern female-empowerment narrative. In practice, however, the film’s narrative logic quickly falls apart. The screenwriting team seems less interested in establishing coherent rules for its universe than in rushing from one action set-piece to the next. Physics, character motivations, and world-building shift entirely on a whim. Susan’s power dynamics fluctuate wildly depending on the needs of a specific scene, rendering her physical strength meaningless whenever the plot requires tension. Furthermore, the film is littered with careless details—government protocols that make no sense even within the bounds of farce, and secondary characters who exist solely as props rather than functioning elements of a living world.

This structural apathy directly undermines the film’s thematic ambitions. *Monsters vs. Aliens* purports to be a story about self-acceptance and rejecting toxic dynamics, as Susan learns to embrace her giant frame and dump her narcissistic fiancé. Yet, this emotional arc feels unearned and formulaic, buried beneath an avalanche of noise. 

Equally disappointing is the film's attempt at satire. A homage to classic creature double-features should offer either a loving, knowledgeable parody of the genre or a sharp critique of modern anxieties. *Monsters vs. Aliens* settles for neither, offering a toothless satire that mistakes references for humor. Gags involving a bumbling, synthesizer-playing U.S. President (Stephen Colbert) spoofing *Close Encounters of the Third Kind* feel dated on arrival and cater to the lowest common denominator. The jokes rely heavily on slapstick and fleeting pop-culture nod-and-winks rather than genuine character-driven comedy. 

This brings to light a recurring, fundamental flaw in DreamWorks’ production model during this era. Rather than building a film around a tightly crafted script and deep emotional core—as contemporaries like Pixar were doing with masterpieces like *WALL-E* and *Up*—DreamWorks routinely prioritized star power and technological novelty. Casting high-profile celebrities like Witherspoon, Rogen, and Colbert guarantees strong marketing hooks, but no amount of star charisma can mask a paper-thin character arc. Similarly, while the stereoscopic 3D rendering was heralded as the future of the medium, the flashy visual effects serve only to distract from the void where the film’s heart ought to be.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is by no means an unwatchable film; its action sequences are slick, its pacing is fast, and young audiences may well be entertained by its brightly colored chaos. But evaluated against higher animation standards, it stands as a hollow spectacle. By prioritizing loud gimmicks over narrative discipline and toothless gags over authentic thematic exploration, DreamWorks created a movie that expands its heroine to massive proportions while leaving its storytelling painfully small.

**CNN.com** — Entertainment

# Review: 'Monsters vs. Aliens' is a 3D exercise in corporate cynicism

**By David Allen, CNN**
**March 27, 2009**

**(CNN) —** If you were to sit in a Hollywood board room with a spreadsheet, a box of crayons, and a desperate mandate to extract an extra four dollars per ticket from exhausted parents, you would arrive at *Monsters vs. Aliens*. 

The latest product off the DreamWorks Animation conveyor belt arrives this weekend not so much as a movie, but as a shiny, 94-minute infomercial for the revival of RealD 3D. It is a film constructed entirely out of pop-culture regurgitation, celebrity voice-cast paychecks, and objects relentlessly poked into the audience’s faces to justify the price of the plastic glasses.

The premise—if one can call a Frankenstein-monster of half-baked homage a premise—begins with Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), a blandly dutiful bride whose primary character trait is her desire to marry a sleazy local TV weatherman (Paul Rudd, doing his usual smug routine on autopilot). On her wedding day, Susan is struck by a radioactive meteor, absorbs a substance called "quantonium," and grows to fifty feet tall. 

Naturally, the U.S. government—represented by a war-mongering general named W.R. Monger (Kiefer Sutherland, barking through his paycheck)—captures her and tosses her into a secret facility. There, she meets a collection of mid-century B-movie knockoffs: a mad scientist cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a prehistoric fish-man (Will Arnett), a 350-foot grub, and a gelatinous blue blob named B.O.B., voiced by Seth Rogen. Rogen plays the blob by simply doing his standard, gravelly Seth Rogen chuckle, proving that character work is strictly optional in modern animation.

When an alien overlord named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) invades Earth to retrieve the quantonium, the President of the United States (Stephen Colbert, playing a caricature that was already feeling tired on basic cable) decides to pit our lovable freaks against the alien menace. 

Chaos ensues. Pixels collide. San Francisco landmarks are systematically destroyed in a manner designed to look impressive on an IMAX screen.

What *Monsters vs. Aliens* lacks is a single frame of genuine warmth or original thought. Where Pixar spends years polishing screenplays to extract genuine human emotion from trash-compacting robots or rat chefs, DreamWorks remains committed to the "shove a pop song over a action sequence" school of filmmaking. The emotional core here is supposed to be Susan’s journey toward self-actualization—learning that she doesn't need her shallow fiancé because she is literally a strong, independent 50-foot woman. But the film’s idea of female empowerment feels as calculated as a corporate diversity seminar, tossed in between jokes about glowing blue goo and paddleballs flying toward the viewer's retina.

To be fair, the technical execution is slick. The digital artists at DreamWorks certainly know how to render sun-dappled Golden Gate Bridge cables and alien spaceship corridors. But it’s a hollow triumph. The film borrows heavily from 1950s sci-fi classics like *The Attack of the 50 Foot Woman* and *The Blob*, but it lacks the cheesy charm or genuine paranoia of those originals. Instead, it weaponizes nostalgia, packaging it for eight-year-olds who won't get the references, and their parents, who will be too distracted by the 3D depth-of-field to care.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* will undoubtedly make millions this weekend. It will sell happy meal toys, launch a video game, and secure a couple of direct-to-DVD holiday specials. But as a piece of cinema, it’s just another loud, bright, plastic distraction. It's not a movie; it's a theme park ride that forgets to be fun.

**Rating: C-**

*Monsters vs. Aliens is rated PG for sci-fi action, some crude humor and mild language. Running time: 94 minutes.*

**Title:** *Monsters vs. Aliens*: Proof That DreamWorks Still Thinks a Pop Song Fixes a Broken Script

**Rating:** ★★☆☆☆ (Two out of five pairs of smudged 3D glasses)

While the fine folks over at Pixar were busy crafting timeless masterpieces about grief, environmental collapse, and the existential dread of aging—you know, *actual cinema*—the executive suite at DreamWorks Animation apparently held a pitch meeting that consisted of a toddler throwing action figures into a blender while blasting 1980s synth-pop. 

The result of that fever dream is *Monsters vs. Aliens*, a 94-minute assault on both the senses and the laws of basic Newtonian physics. 

The plot, if we dare dignify it with such a word, follows Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon, playing "plucky blonde" for the thousandth time), who is struck by a meteor on her wedding day, turns 50 feet tall, and is immediately thrown into a secret government facility. There, she meets a ragtag crew of classic B-movie homage rejects: a brainless gelatinous blob named B.O.B. (Seth Rogen doing his usual "chuckle through the lines" schtick), a mad-scientist cockroach (Hugh Laurie), and a fish-man missing link (Will Arnett). Naturally, when a generic alien warlord attacks Earth, the military decides these freaks are humanity’s only hope.

Now, let’s talk about DreamWorks’ favorite trope: the frantic, desperate reliance on pop-culture references to hide a complete lack of soul. Where a Pixar film builds a world with internal logic and emotional weight, *Monsters vs. Aliens* just points at an 80s movie and waits for the parents in the audience to clap like trained seals. 

Case in point: Stephen Colbert plays the President of the United States. How does he attempt to communicate with the invading alien robot? By playing Harold Faltermeyer’s "Axel F" (yes, the *Beverly Hills Cop* theme) on a Yamaha synthesizer, culminating in a *Close Encounters of the Third Kind* gag. It’s not witty; it’s a pop-culture roll call. It’s the cinematic equivalent of a jingling set of keys meant to distract a hyperactive child.

And then we come to the physics. Oh, the physics. 

Look, I understand it’s a cartoon. But Pixar understands that for fantasy to work, it needs ground rules. *The Incredibles* played with super-strength, but objects still had perceived weight and mass. In *Monsters vs. Aliens*, the writers seem to think mass is just a suggestion. When Susan—now weighing several tons—runs through the streets of San Francisco using two Chevrolet Corvettes as roller skates, the Golden Gate Bridge collapses not because of actual kinetic stress, but simply because the scene needed a set-piece. Gravity is routinely suspended whenever a slapstick gag calls for it, and the square-cube law isn't just ignored; it’s actively insulted. Susan should have crushed her own spine the second she stood up, but instead, she pulls off gymnastics maneuvers that would make Spider-Man sweat.

The movie’s entire selling point was its "groundbreaking" 3D technology, which translates to a paddleball routinely being hit directly into the camera lens. It’s cheap gimmickry, designed to make you pay an extra four dollars at the box office for the privilege of a headache.

Is it entirely unwatchable? No. Seth Rogen’s brainless blob gets a chuckle or two simply because Rogen’s vocal delivery is bulletproof, and the visual design of the monsters is retro-cute. But it’s hollow. It’s loud, fast, hyperactive, and utterly forgettable. 

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is the ultimate manifestation of the DreamWorks assembly line: take a handful of celebrity voice actors, add a dash of 1950s nostalgia, drown it in licensed music, throw physics out the window, and pray nobody notices the script is paper-thin. 

If you want a movie that treats animation as an art form, go re-watch *WALL-E*. If you want a 90-minute babysitter that thinks a giant insect sneezing on a general is the height of comedy, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is waiting in the bargain bin.

**CNN.com** | Entertainment

# Review: 'Monsters vs. Aliens' turns classic B-movie sci-fi into a 3D spectacle

By **Tom Coates**, CNN  
March 27, 2009

**(CNN)** — DreamWorks Animation has built an empire on pop-culture parodies and irreverent humor, but with *[Monsters vs. Aliens](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/movies)*, the studio sets its sights on a specific, nostalgic niche: the creature features and alien invasion flicks of the 1950s. 

The result is a fast-paced, visually stunning comedy that trades cheap gags for genuine affection for cinema history. Powered by impressive 3D technology and a standout lead performance, the film manages to be both a clever homage to sci-fi classics and a genuinely fun family blockbuster.

***

### Ginormica: A towering heroine with heart

At the center of the story is Susan Murphy, a modest Modesto woman whose dream wedding is interrupted when she is struck by a radioactive meteor. Absorbing the alien substance Quantonium, Susan grows to a staggering 49 feet and 11 inches tall, prompting the U.S. military to capture her, rename her "Ginormica," and lock her away in a secret government facility.

Voiced with infectious warmth and grit by [Reese Witherspoon](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/celebrities/reese-witherspoon), Ginormica is the emotional anchor of the movie. Rather than treating her size as merely a punchline, the script allows her to undergo a compelling arc. She evolves from a meek woman trying to fit into her self-absorbed fiancé’s small-town life into a confident powerhouse who embraces her strength. Witherspoon's vocal performance strikes the right balance between vulnerable and heroic, making Ginormica one of DreamWorks’ most refreshing female protagonists to date.

***

### A voice cast that breathes life into the monster mash

While Witherspoon grounds the film, the supporting voice cast leans fully into the absurdity. The misfit group of monsters imprisoned alongside Ginormica steals nearly every scene they are in:

* **[Seth Rogen](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/celebrities/seth-rogen)** is inspired casting as B.O.B. (Benzoate Ostylezene Bicarbonate), a gelatinous, brainless mass who provides the film's biggest laughs. Rogen’s signature upbeat energy makes the indestructible blob utterly lovable.
* **Hugh Laurie** brings a hilarious, dry sophistication to Dr. Cockroach Ph.D., a mad scientist who accidentally turned himself into a insect-headed genius.
* **[Will Arnett](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/celebrities/will-arnett)** shines as The Missing Link, a 20,000-year-old fish-man who fancies himself a macho beach hunk, despite being completely out of his element.
* **Kiefer Sutherland** delivers a standout voice performance as General W.R. Monger, a gruff, gravel-voiced military commander straight out of a Cold War propaganda film. 

Opposing our monster heroes is the grandstanding alien overlord Gallaxhar, voiced with delightfully campy villainy by [Rainn Wilson](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/celebrities/rainn-wilson). Special credit also goes to [Paul Rudd](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/celebrities/paul-rudd), who turns Susan’s self-centered news-anchor fiancé Derek into a character you love to hate.

***

### A love letter to classic sci-fi homages

Film buffs will find a lot to love in *Monsters vs. Aliens*. The movie is saturated with affection for [1950s sci-fi cinema](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/movies/sci-fi-history), pulling directly from iconic creature features:

* Ginormica is a clear nod to *Attack of the 50 Foot Woman* (1958).
* B.O.B. reimagines the terrifying titular monster from *The Blob* (1958).
* Dr. Cockroach spoofs Vincent Price's classic transformation in *The Fly* (1958).
* The Missing Link plays on *Creature from the Black Lagoon* (1954).
* The giant silkworm, Insectosaurus, evokes Japan's classic *Mothra* and *Godzilla* kaiju traditions.

Beyond creature design, the film drops hysterical references to modern sci-fi classics. A scene where the President of the United States attempts to communicate with the alien robot using a synthesizer keyboard is a hilarious riff on Steven Spielberg’s *[Close Encounters of the Third Kind](https://www.cnn.com/entertainment/movies)*, while the military command center echoes Stanley Kubrick's *Dr. Strangelove*.

***

### Visuals: Native 3D that sets a new standard

*Monsters vs. Aliens* marks a major milestone for DreamWorks as their first film shot natively in 3D (using the [InTru3D format](https://www.cnn.com/tech)) rather than retrofitted in post-production. The difference is immediately clear. 

The stereoscopic visuals aren't just used for cheap gimmicks (though a paddle-ball gag early on reminds viewers they are watching a 3D movie). Instead, the depth of field is used to accentuate scale. When Ginormica barrels down the streets of San Francisco using sports cars as roller skates, the sense of altitude, speed, and spatial depth is genuinely thrilling. The centerpiece action sequence on the Golden Gate Bridge is worth the price of admission alone, standing out as one of the best-executed animated set pieces in recent memory.

***

### The Verdict

*Monsters vs. Aliens* doesn't break new ground in terms of narrative structure, but it executes its premise with so much energy, visual flair, and heart that it’s hard not to be charmed. Fueled by Reese Witherspoon's strong lead performance and a technical team firing on all cylinders, DreamWorks has delivered a monster movie that operates as both a sharp satire for adults and a roaring adventure for kids.

**CNN Rating:** 3 out of 4 stars (Worth the 3D ticket upgrade)

*Monsters vs. Aliens is rated PG for sci-fi action, some crude humor, and mild language. Running time: 94 minutes.*

This time, the culprit arrives loaded with every tired trope in the studio’s play-it-safe handbook: an insecure, fast-talking protagonist who learns to "just be himself," an overly enthusiastic comic-relief sidekick, and a jukebox soundtrack packed with enough forced pop hits to make a wedding DJ wince.

They bounce through a script relying heavily on two things: pop-culture references that will be hopelessly outdated by next Tuesday, and enough bodily-function jokes to ensure the under-eight demographic stays placated.

Millions of dollars have clearly been poured into making every hair, scale, and background detail shine with pristine, photorealistic beauty. Kids will no doubt be dazzled by the bright colors and sugar-rush pacing, but parents forced to tag along should prepare for an excruciating exercise in endurance. Consider yourselves warned.

**Monsters vs. Aliens: A Soulless Monument to Hollywood’s Hollowest Impulse**

DreamWorks Animation’s 2009 release, *Monsters vs. Aliens*, stands as a masterclass in corporate cynicism—a film built entirely on pitch-deck buzzwords, glossy tech demos, and a star-studded cast list, but completely devoid of a soul. On paper, the high-concept elevator pitch is undeniably fun: a loving, retro homage to 1950s B-movie creature features, where classic cinema monsters are conscripted by the U.S. government to fight an alien invasion. 

In practice, however, the film is a catastrophic reminder that no amount of flashy gimmickry, 3D visual effects, or A-list celebrity voice talent can save a script that is dead on arrival.

The primary failure of *Monsters vs. Aliens* lies in its abysmal screenplay. Written by a committee of five screenwriters—a red flag in any production—the script abandons the witty parodic potential of its premise in favor of frantic noise, low-hanging pop-culture references, and agonizingly predictable beats. The emotional arc of its protagonist, Susan Murphy (a.k.a. Ginormica), is so by-the-numbers it feels generated by an algorithm. Her journey toward self-worth after being dumped by a vain weather reporter is buried under a barrage of Michael Bay-lite action sequences. Rather than delivering clever satirical jabs at the cold-war anxieties that spawned the original 1950s sci-fi genre, the writing settles for lazy, recycled gags and frantic physical comedy designed solely to keep hyperactive children from looking away from the screen.

Even more egregious is the wasted talent standing behind the microphone. DreamWorks’ obsession with stunt-casting celebrity names over actual voice actors has rarely yielded such diminished returns. Reese Witherspoon delivers a lead performance so flat and earnest it drains the energy out of every scene she is in. Seth Rogen simply plays his usual persona—giggly, loud, and stoner-adjacent—trapped inside a blue gelatinous blob. Hugh Laurie and Will Arnett, two of the sharpest comedic minds in modern television, are utterly squandered, reduced to delivering lines that sound like first-draft filler. Stephen Colbert’s brief stint as the President yields a few mild chuckles, but a single decent bit in a 90-minute film is not a victory; it is a tragedy of wasted opportunity.

The film relies heavily on its visual presentation to distract from these structural failings. It was famously pushed as a pioneer in modern 3D cinema, but this focus only highlights its lack of depth. The movie constantly pauses its narrative momentum to thrust objects directly into the camera lens, prioritizing cheap carnivalesque parlor tricks over atmospheric storytelling or character development.

When a film fails this spectacularly on a narrative level, it loses the right to its pretensions. *Monsters vs. Aliens* cost an astronomical $175 million to manufacture, yet it possesses less charm, heart, and genuine humor than films made for a fraction of its budget. 

In fact, if forced to choose between this bloated, cynical product and *Space Chimps*—the universally mocked 2008 budget animation about primates in space—the chimps win hands down. Where *Monsters vs. Aliens* is weighed down by its own self-importance, massive budget, and desperate plea for blockbuster status, *Space Chimps* at least possessed the good grace to be unpretentious. It was silly, absurd, and entirely aware of its own stupidity. It didn't try to dazzle you with A-list voice actors who sounded like they were reading their lines during a drive-thru run, nor did it hide a broken script behind $100 million worth of flashy explosions. 

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is a shiny, empty shell of a movie—a textbook example of Hollywood believing that a high concept and a red-carpet cast can replace actual storytelling. It is noisy, forgettable, and aggressively mediocre. Skip the monsters, ignore the aliens, and leave this relic in the bargain bin where it belongs. At least the chimps had the decency to be fun.
